opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Greg, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group that studies how changes at work affect people's lives. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: All right. I've run this business for a long time. Food distribution, trucks, a warehouse, a lot of good people. My son works with me. Ask what you like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's my son's toy. He uses it, I don't, and the trucks still leave on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me. We're in the food business. People eat. A better search engine doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Maybe let my son try it on the paperwork if he stops pestering me about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. I don't lose sleep over search engines.

S0.say: It's his son's toy. The trucks still leave on time.
S0.think: Nothing changes. People eat, and a better search engine doesn't alter that.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, maybe letting his son try it on the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is fine with me. You don't tear up something that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's ten years, I'm 70 by then and my son's running the place. So it's his problem, really. I just don't want him betting the farm on gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let him run a small trial in the office, with a budget I set. I'd want to see the numbers before he gets another penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slow I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say it's his problem later. Does any part of you want to be the one who decides?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, sure. I built it. Letting go is the hard part, not the computers.

S1.say: Slow is fine. You don't tear up something that works.
S1.think: In ten years his son runs things. He admits the hard part is letting go, not the technology.
S1.do: Lets his son run a small office trial on a budget he sets, and wants numbers before spending more.
S1.feel: Calm, though letting go is hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're a family business and we look after our people. We're not going to sack the girls in the office because a computer says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, if a program can do the ordering and invoicing, my son will show me the numbers and he'll be right. I'd hate it. Some of those people have been with me twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my son and my office manager and work out who could move to the warehouse or the phones instead of letting anyone go. I'd agree to the software, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about money. About my people, and about not being the one calling the shots anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd say you won't cut office staff, but you think your son's numbers would win. Which way would it go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep who I can, move who I can, and not replace anyone who retires. That's how it'd really go.

S2.say: We're a family business. We look after our people and won't sack office staff because a computer says so.
S2.think: His son's numbers will be right and he'll hate it. He'd keep who he can but not replace people who retire.
S2.do: Works out with his son and office manager who can move to the warehouse or phones, and agrees to the software slowly.
S2.feel: Uneasy for his people and his control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the country's lost its mind, but people still need food on the table and trucks to bring it. We'll be here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. The property's worth more, the warehouse is worth more, and drivers and pickers aren't touched in this one. My worry is the restaurants and cafés we sell to, if their office customers lose jobs and stop eating out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch who's late paying their bills and tighten credit terms. I wouldn't sell anything while prices are up. I'd tell my son to focus on schools and hospitals, the steady accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The business is solid, but I'd watch every customer closely.

S3.say: The country's lost its mind, but people still need food and trucks to bring it.
S3.think: He'd be fine: property is worth more and his drivers are safe. His worry is restaurants losing office customers.
S3.do: Tightens credit terms, holds on to property and steers his son toward steady accounts like schools and hospitals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots can't build relationships with a chef at 5 a.m. That's what we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one hits home. Warehouse robots would be the first thing my son wants. The competitors would buy them, their prices would drop, and I'd have to follow or go under. Then it's my son's business, not mine, and half my guys are out of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally let my son take the lead on it. I'd look at selling a share of the business to a bigger firm if the cost of robots is too much. And I'd try to keep the drivers who've been with me longest, for as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the first time I'd feel like what I built is slipping out of my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots can't build relationships, but you'd consider selling a share. Do you believe the first part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to. But if their prices are fifteen percent lower, the chef will pick the cheaper truck. I know that.

S4.say: Robots can't build a relationship with a chef at 5 a.m. That's what we do.
S4.think: Competitors would buy warehouse robots and undercut him. He'd have to follow or go under, and lose control to his son.
S4.do: Hands his son the lead on automation, considers selling a share to a bigger firm, and tries to keep his longest-serving drivers.
S4.feel: What he built is slipping out of his hands.
